title: Al-Mumit, the Taker of Life
tomorrow: the day the Prophet died, what did Abu Bakr say?

lines: THE NEWS, IN A GROUP CHAT.
cards: News of a death often arrives the modern way now, in a group chat, and the replies stack up: so sorry, hearts, a praying-hands emoji.

A Muslim's reply may begin with one sentence before anything else: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Here's the odd part.
Someone has just died, and the sentence isn't about them. It says we. And it doesn't say will return.

teach.b: The puzzle solves itself once you read where the sentence lives.

In Surah al-Baqarah, Allah says people will be tested with fear and hunger and loss of wealth and lives and harvests, and gives good news to the patient, those who say, when a misfortune strikes them, this sentence.
So first: it's for any misfortune, not only a death. And second: the we is the point.
The one saying it puts themselves inside the grief. Nobody stands outside it handing out comfort.
Everyone in that group chat is on the same road, and returning means already on the way, all of us, right now. Today's Name is Al-Mumit, the one who gives death, the Taker of Life.
In Surah al-Mulk, Pickthall: "Who hath created life and death that He may try you which of you is best in conduct."
Death there is created. It's not an accident in the system, or an enemy that slipped in. It's His, the same as life.
Here's what's worth telling a friend tonight: the sentence Muslims say at a death is in the first person plural. It quietly counts the speaker in.

how: On hearing of a death or any loss, Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, and the janazah, the funeral prayer, is prayed together for the one who died.

o: the judge who weighs a life at its end
the one who causes death, and holds it
the angel who carries away each soul

games.q: the sentence and the Name — tap the pairs.
p: and unto Him we are returning

s: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un is a sentence about the person who died
it says 'we': we are Allah's, and unto Him we are returning. it counts the speaker in.
the Qur'an gives this sentence for any misfortune, not only a death
the patient say it "when a misfortune striketh them."
Surah al-Mulk says death was created
"Who hath created life and death that He may try you which of you is best in conduct."

games.q: your coach's father died. the team chat fills with 'rip' and hearts. you want to say something real, in the spirit of today's verse. which fits best?
o: 'we're with you, coach. we're all on this road together.'
nothing; death is too private for a group chat.
games.why: the verse says 'we' and 'returning': nobody grieves from outside. a Muslim might write inna lillahi; to anyone, the 'we' can be said in plain words.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable. Bring to mind someone you've lost, or simply the fact that every life, yours included, is on its way back. On the in-breath, we are Allah's; on the out-breath, to Him we are returning.
If it gets heavy, open your eyes and rest them on something near you; peaceful is the aim, not hard.

wordCard.voice: Al-Mumit. The Taker of Life: the one who created death along with life, and holds both.

orig.note: Arabic: the one who gives death; in the list of the Names it comes right after Al-Muhyi, the Giver of Life.

carryVoice: Hold it gently: death is his, and so it's a return, not a cliff. Day fifteen thirty-five, held.
